concept: Fast trading signals: order flow funding open interest liquidations and data APIs
summary: Source-anchored research for Fast trading signals: order flow funding open interest liquidations and data APIs. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Combining OI with funding (CoinMarketMan heuristic, untested): rising OI with high positive funding means longs are paying shorts to hold, so the trend may be better to fade than chase; OI and funding together indicate whether crowd positioning is sustainable. (low confidence)

Hyperliquid's liquidation chain differs in detail. Below maintenance margin, the engine sends market orders to the order book. For positions above 100k USDC it sends 20% per attempt, and for 30 seconds after a partial liquidation it sends the whole position. Below 2/3 of maintenance margin, the liquidator vault (part of HLP) can take the position over, and the user's maintenance margin is not returned. ADL is the last step. It ranks opposing users by (mark_price / entry_price) * (notional_position / account_value) and closes them at the previous mark price. Inference: a large cluster at one price can therefore unwind in tranches, not as one order. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

In Hudson and Urquhart's daily data the edge sits on the long side. The average return from a buy signal is positive and significant for every coin and rule class, and over 90% of rules have positive buy returns for Litecoin, Ripple and both Bitcoin series. Sell-signal (short) returns are mostly negative, and in 15 of 20 rule-class-by-coin cells no rule earns a significant sell return. The sample is a strong uptrend, so part of this may be market drift. (low confidence)

PBO needs the full set of trials. Hiding trials makes the test understate overfitting (the authors compare it to removing non-responders from a drug trial), and for guided searches the matrix columns should hold each search's final converged result, not its intermediate steps. Bailey and López de Prado add that PBO is non-parametric but 'requires a large amount of information'. The PBO paper also lists design limits: strong autocorrelation in the performance series can make the symmetric block division obscure it, especially when S is large. (medium confidence)

Keep a trial ledger from the first experiment: every signal variant, feature, horizon, asset and threshold tried, with its full P&L series, failures included. The ledger supplies N, the variance of trial Sharpe ratios for DSR, and the T-by-N matrix that PBO needs. Bailey and López de Prado say investors and referees should demand the trial count, and that multiple-testing exercises should be planned in advance because each extra trial raises the false-positive probability. Whether correlated variants count as one trial or many is a judgement to disclose. (medium confidence)

Do not read a bright band as a price target or a timing signal. CoinGlass calls dense zones 'magnetic zones' that price may gravitate toward. Hyblock lists the magnet reading beside support, resistance and reversal readings. MMT says a map shows where orders sit, not when they trigger, that a cluster can stay untouched indefinitely, and that once clusters are visible, participants may avoid them or target them. The three pages cite no test of the magnet effect. (high confidence)

A signal's decay speed (its half-life) sets how hard to trade it. In Garleanu and Pedersen's model, predictors with slower mean reversion ('alpha decay') get more weight in the aim portfolio, and an investor facing transaction costs trades more aggressively on persistent signals than on fast mean-reverting ones, because the benefits of persistent signals accrue over longer periods. Without trading costs the optimal portfolio does not depend on alpha decay. The paper's empirical test uses commodity futures with 5-day, 12-month and 5-year signals, not intraday data. (medium confidence)

Record both the exchange event time and your own receive time; their gap is a direct latency measurement. CoinAPI defines time_exchange (stamped by the exchange) and time_coinapi (stamped on arrival at its ingestion point), calls the difference the 'latency fingerprint' of an event, recommends time_coinapi for latency measurement and cross-exchange sequencing, and sets time_exchange equal to time_coinapi when the exchange sends no timestamp. An open-source feed handler's FAQ likewise records the local machine clock by default and warns that not all API messages carry an exchange timestamp, especially order records. (medium confidence)

Over short intervals the mid-price change is roughly linear in OFI, and the fit is contemporaneous (same interval), not a forecast. Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov regress mid-price change on OFI over 10-second intervals for 50 US stocks (NYSE TAQ). Xu, Gould and Howison fit a linear model of contemporaneous mid-price change on multi-level OFI for 6 Nasdaq stocks. Bugaenko, in equity data, reports that price impact grows linearly with order-flow imbalance for small signed order flows. (high confidence)

Coinbase warns that messages can be dropped from the matches channel and recommends tracking the last trade ID through the heartbeat channel and fetching missed trades from REST. Inference, not stated by Coinbase: because CVD is a running sum, an unrepaired gap leaves a permanent offset in every later CVD value. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Imbalance carries more information when the tick is large relative to price. Gould and Bonart report considerable improvement in direction classification for large-tick stocks and only moderate improvement for small-tick stocks. Bieganowski and Slepaczuk report that the predictive effect of imbalance (SHAP) is stronger for instruments with larger ticks. Implication to test: expect a cleaner OBI signal on coarse-tick pairs than on very fine-tick ones. (medium confidence)

Hudson and Urquhart's best in-sample rules lost money out of sample for Bitcoin. The in-sample winners were channel-breakout rules for both Bitcoin series and Litecoin, and moving-average rules for Ripple and Ethereum. In January to June 2018 both Bitcoin series had negative annualized return, Sharpe and Sortino ratios, while the other three coins stayed positive. The window is six months long and falls in a bear market, so it is a weak test in either direction. The authors suggest Bitcoin is more efficient because more investors watch it. (low confidence)

Constrain the search with theory before computing anything. Bailey and López de Prado say investment theory, not computational power, should decide which experiments are worth running, and suggest an optimal-stopping rule: sample roughly 37% of the theoretically justified configurations, then take the first that beats all of them. Harvey, Liu and Zhu say a factor derived from first principles can face a lower hurdle than one found by empirical search. For order-flow or funding signals, a mechanism written down before the test shrinks N and defends a lower bar; that application is an inference from the two papers. (medium confidence)

Pull oracles hand freshness control to the consumer. Pyth Core advertises '500+ feeds with 400ms updates across 100+ chains': the app fetches a signed price from the off-chain Hermes service and submits it on-chain for verification in the same transaction. Chainlink Data Streams generates reports continuously off-chain 'on a sub-second basis' and the app fetches them on demand. The Chainlink pages reviewed state no millisecond latency figure. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Input representation matters more than model depth. Kolm et al. find models trained on order flow (stationary inputs derived from the book) significantly outperform most models trained directly on raw order book states (115 Nasdaq stocks). Xu et al. find the out-of-sample fit of the contemporaneous OFI relationship improves with each added price level (6 Nasdaq stocks). Wang (Bybit BTC/USDT snapshots at 100 ms to multi-second intervals) reports simpler models can match or beat deeper networks when preprocessing is good. (medium confidence)

Kitron and Wengrowicz test the 15-minute reversal against measurement artifacts (their package includes flat-bar-excluded and one-bar-gap refits) and report that it survives, but the effect is small. The class-mean AUC gap between crypto and equities is +0.031 as designed and +0.011 (95% CI +0.008 to +0.014) under the most conservative accounting. The result also survives an exact permutation null and a frozen holdout. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-22)

Elevated basis or funding is a crowding gauge, not a timing tool. BIS finds high crypto carry predicts future price crashes and that rising carry goes with a rising price of crash-risk insurance. CoinMarketMan reads rising OI plus extreme funding plus a nearby liquidation cluster as an overcrowded market at risk of a sharp reversal, while saying it does not give the timing. (medium confidence)

Funding-rate arbitrage is not risk-free and earns mostly from convergence. He et al.: the perp cash-and-carry has no predetermined unwind date; in their decomposition price convergence dominates strategy returns while funding payments play a minor, diminishing role; their no-arbitrage result is conditional on exchange solvency. BIS: the arbitrage side is risky because margins spike and liquidations hit in drawdowns, which keeps arbitrage capital scarce. (medium confidence)

A backtest's Sharpe ratio cannot be interpreted without the number of independent trials behind it. Even if every strategy has zero true skill, the best Sharpe among N independent trials rises with N, so more searching produces better-looking winners; Bailey and López de Prado give an extreme-value approximation for this expected maximum. They call the number of trials attempted the most important piece of information missing from virtually all published backtests, and say a backtest whose author has not controlled for the extent of the search is 'worthless, regardless of how excellent the reported performance might be'. Harvey, Liu and Zhu make the same point from the other side: failed tests are never published, so the number of factors tested is unobservable. (high confidence)

The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) is a Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio whose rejection threshold is raised to reflect the multiplicity of trials. Beyond the mean and standard deviation of returns it needs five more inputs: skewness, kurtosis, sample length T, the variance of Sharpe ratios across trials, and the number of independent trials N. Non-normality matters because negative skew and fat tails can inflate a Sharpe ratio; Harvey and Liu raise the same caveat for option-like strategies with negative skew. (medium confidence)

Fill and latency assumptions can erase a fast signal's edge, and a replay backtest cannot test them. HftBacktest's documentation says a market-data replay cannot change the market, so one of the most important assumptions is that your order is small enough to have no impact; some partial-fill cases and large liquidity-taking fills may be unrealistic; and you must test in a live market and adjust the backtest to the discrepancies. For passive orders it offers a conservative RiskAverseQueueModel (queue position advances only when a trade prints at your price) and a probabilistic ProbQueueModel. It supports only market-by-price depth, which most crypto venues provide, so queue position must be estimated. It also separates feed latency (handled with local and exchange timestamps), order-entry latency and order-response latency. (medium confidence)

Vendors advise using the map as a relative risk gauge. CoinGlass says to pair it with market depth and open interest, to match the lookback (12 hours to one year) to the holding period, and that a dense zone with thin depth may see sharp moves or quick reversals while a dense zone with strong depth may see smoother moves. Hyblock says to compare sizes with other levels, not to read them as absolute amounts. (medium confidence)

Price-versus-OI read (a descriptive heuristic, not a forecast): price up and OI up = new longs, trend confirmed; price up and OI down = short covering, weaker rally; price down and OI up = new shorts, bearish conviction building; price down and OI down = longs exiting or liquidated, possible exhaustion. CoinMarketMan adds that the rate of change in OI matters more than its level and that sharp OI spikes or drops are events. (medium confidence)

Funding mostly follows price instead of leading it. Presto Research (BTC on Binance, roughly 2021 to 2024): the 7-day change in annualised funding explains 12.5% of contemporaneous price-change variance, but at lag T to T+1 correlation and R-squared are about zero; it concludes single-asset price changes cannot be reliably predicted from funding-rate changes alone. He et al. likewise find trailing spot returns positively predict the perp-spot deviation. (medium confidence)

The cleanest out-of-sample evidence is a forward test of the exact strategy on new data. Harvey and Liu say a true out-of-sample test of the particular strategy, as opposed to a hold-out of historical data, is cleaner but unavailable for most strategies. HftBacktest's documentation says a replay-based result must be checked in a live market with real participants and the backtest adjusted to the gap. For a fast signal this points to a small, logged shadow or live run whose fills, fees and latency are compared with the backtest's assumptions before sizing up. (medium confidence)

Overfitting can be worse than zero skill. Bailey and López de Prado argue that for financial series with memory, the extreme in-sample patterns that backtest overfitting selects are later undone, so overfitting leads to 'loss maximization' out of sample rather than merely no gain. Harvey and Liu, summarising López de Prado and coauthors, say only seven trials are needed to obtain a spurious two-year backtest with an in-sample Sharpe ratio above 1.0 while the expected out-of-sample Sharpe ratio is zero. (medium confidence)

On a venue with public positions, a vendor can compute liquidation levels instead of modeling them. MMT says it runs its own Hyperliquid node and shows the actual liquidation prices of open positions, and it calls conventional CEX heatmaps estimates. Even there, the level is conditional. Hyperliquid's docs say a shown liquidation price can differ from the real one because of funding payments and PnL changes in other cross-margin positions. The docs publish the formula liq_price = price - side * margin_available / position_size / (1 - l * side), where l = 1 / MAINTENANCE_LEVERAGE and the maintenance leverage follows the margin tier at the liquidation price. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Intraday responses to whale events are measured from the public alert, last minutes, and in one study appear only when the alert is published. The Philadelphia Fed paper timestamps events at the Whale Alert broadcast so that its estimates capture 'market responses to the dissemination of information on whale activity rather than to the underlying transactions themselves', and retail reaction concentrates in the first 15 minutes. Saggu (Finance Research Letters, 2022, summarised by the Blockchain Research Lab) reports Bitcoin rising 0.4% at 5 minutes, 0.5% at 10, 0.6% at 15 and 0.8% at 30 after a $1 billion USDT mint, but says price does not significantly change on mints alone and responds when Whale Alert tweets the event. Inference: a signal built on a public alert feed competes with every other subscriber and should be expected to decay within minutes. (medium confidence)

Latency-arbitrage windows shrink as competition for speed rises, but the prize per opportunity does not. In E-mini S&P 500 futures versus the SPY ETF, the median arbitrage duration fell from 97 ms in 2005 to 7 ms in 2011, while median profit stayed about 0.08 index points per unit traded; the authors conclude the speed race 'just continually raises the bar for capturing' the opportunities. A Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond summary reports the same 97 ms to 7 ms decline with unchanged profit per opportunity. (high confidence)

CVD (cumulative volume delta) is the running sum of per-bar delta, where delta = taker (aggressor) buy volume minus taker sell volume. Only the aggressing side of each trade is counted, so unlike total volume it is signed. Because it is a running sum, its level depends on where the window starts; the change over a window is what carries information. (high confidence)

Intraday momentum and reversal switch with market state. Wen et al. report that Bitcoin's intraday predictability pattern changes around large intraday price jumps, FOMC announcements, liquidity levels and the COVID-19 outbreak. A timing strategy built on their intraday predictors earns more economic value than always-long or buy-and-hold. Shen et al. find momentum strongest in high-volume, high-volatility sessions. Both studies point toward conditioning the momentum-or-reversal bet on volatility, volume, jump and liquidity state instead of running one static rule. (medium confidence)

Venue differences matter for cross-venue divergence. BitMEX's own Q3 2025 study (BitMEX, Binance, Hyperliquid) says BitMEX funding was the most stable and Hyperliquid showed much higher funding volatility. The study is BitMEX partner content and promotes the company. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-10-14)

Multiple-testing statistics fix selection bias only; they do not check that the backtest is correct. The PBO paper says its procedure 'does nothing to evaluate the correctness of a backtest', and names incorrect transaction costs and use of data not available at decision time as errors that would feed it flawed information. Harvey and Liu state that the Sharpe ratios in their worked examples reflect no transaction costs, so they are overstated 'before-costs' figures. Remove cost, fill, latency and timestamp errors first, then count trials and deflate the net, decision-time-correct returns. (high confidence)

Do not trust equal-weighted or small, illiquid universe backtests. Novy-Marx and Velikov find anomaly spreads are often larger in smaller stocks, but those stocks are much costlier to trade, so equal-weighted results are 'misleading and should be viewed skeptically' and often show worse net performance. By analogy (an inference, not tested in the paper), a signal that looks strongest on thin altcoin perpetuals deserves the most cost and impact scrutiny. (low confidence)

A passing PBO does not certify the regime, and a high PBO does not prove absence of skill. The PBO paper says the procedure accounts for structural breaks only if they occur inside the dataset; if a break lies outside it, the strategy may be overfit to one regime and PBO will not show it, so the data must be representative of future states. If all tested strategies have high and similar Sharpe ratios, none stands out and PBO is high even though skill exists. (low confidence)

Centralized-exchange liquidation heatmaps are vendor models, not observed position books. Hyblock and CoinGlass both say they compute liquidation levels from market data and assumed leverage levels, then add the results to price buckets. The pages reviewed do not publish the leverage tiers, the entry-price assumptions or the bucket width. (high confidence)

Vendors describe the output as a relative, predicted intensity, not a count of real liquidations. Hyblock says its heatmap predicts where liquidation levels open but not where they close, so the actual number of liquidations will be lower, and that sizes should be read relative to other levels. CoinGlass calls its output a relative intensity indicator and says actual liquidations may be smaller than shown. (high confidence)

Coverage is partial. The Hyblock page reviewed lists Binance Futures, BitMEX and Bybit with BTC and ETH products only. MMT says its Hyperliquid map describes the participants on that exchange, not the whole market. A cluster is therefore a statement about a subset of venues. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

On-chain wallet tracking is adversarial. Luo et al. report that bots 'front-run trades, conceal positions, and fabricate sentiment' in meme-coin copy trading, that bundle bots appear in roughly one quarter of projects, and that gradual bundles 'obscure temporal signals and attribution', making them much harder to detect. (low confidence)

The two big oracle vendors match push and pull to different jobs. Chainlink describes push Data Feeds as suited to lending and liquidations and pull Data Streams to latency-sensitive uses such as perps. Pyth draws the same line: Pyth Pro contracts verify a signed price on each transaction and store none (used for perps and RFQ), while Pyth Core contracts verify and store the price, which stays available until a newer update replaces it (used for lending markets, CDPs and vaults). (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Fast-signal backtests that omit latency report an upper bound. The Binance perpetual study states 'Latency is not explicitly modeled; results should be interpreted as an upper bound in the fastest regime', and says real execution faces latency, network jitter and queue position effects that are hard to simulate. (low confidence)

Oracle price updates are themselves a tradeable event. Oracle Extractable Value (OEV) is MEV captured by back-running oracle updates, chiefly liquidations in lending markets. Chainlink SVR (introduced December 2024) auctions the right to liquidate, and the protocol briefly holds back publishing the updated price to run the auction, so the on-chain price is deliberately delayed. UMA's Oval estimated that Aave missed about $62 million of revenue over three years by not capturing OEV; this is an estimate, not a measured loss. (medium confidence)

Forward-looking evidence on book imbalance sits at very short horizons. Gould and Bonart predict the direction of the next mid-price move from queue imbalance (10 Nasdaq stocks). Kolm, Turiel and Westray find the effective horizon of stock-specific forecasts is about two average price changes (115 Nasdaq stocks). Bieganowski and Slepaczuk use a 3-second log mid-price return target on 1-second Binance perpetual data. Horizon half-life is owned by a sibling concept; this claim only records the horizons the studies tested. (medium confidence)

OFI is computed from best-quote updates. Per book event, e_n = I{P^B_n >= P^B_(n-1)} q^B_n - I{P^B_n <= P^B_(n-1)} q^B_(n-1) - I{P^A_n <= P^A_(n-1)} q^A_n + I{P^A_n >= P^A_(n-1)} q^A_(n-1), where P is the best price, q the best size, B bid, A ask, and I the indicator function. OFI over an interval is the sum of e_n. Multi-level OFI (MLOFI) extends this to a vector over price levels. (medium confidence)

Venues encode trade direction differently, so a multi-venue CVD must normalise the sign per venue. Binance m says whether the buyer was the maker (true means the taker sold). Coinbase Exchange match messages put the MAKER order side in 'side': 'sell' means the maker sold, the match is an up-tick, and the taker bought. Bybit v5 public trade field S is documented as 'Side of taker'. Treating the three alike flips delta on some venues. (high confidence)

Build the coin universe point-in-time. Zarattini et al. use a survivorship-bias-free dataset of all coins traded since 2015 and trade the 20 most liquid. Grobys et al. fix the 30 largest coins by market capitalization at the end of each prior December to avoid illiquid small coins, which Zaremba et al. link to daily reversal. These choices target survivorship bias and illiquid-coin artifacts. (medium confidence)

Near-zero autocorrelation does not rule out a reversal edge. In the Kitron and Wengrowicz data, lag-one return autocorrelation is near zero on major coins, yet a rule that bets against the sign of the previous 15-minute candle captures most of the effect. The authors write that the signal lives in signs, not magnitudes. A linear autocorrelation test alone can therefore miss it. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-22)
